hook: Finding an area by stacking millions of thin rectangles sounds hopeless by hand. Yet $\int_1^3 (3x^2 - 2)\,dx$ takes four lines: find a function whose derivative is $3x^2 - 2$, plug in 3 and 1, subtract. That shortcut, the second half of the Fundamental Theorem, is why calculus can compute areas, distances and totals at all.

prereq.why: $g'(x) = f(x)$, so $g$ is an antiderivative of $f$.

ideas: FTC, part 2: if $F' = f$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) = F(x)\Big|_a^b$.
Net change: $\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)$, so $f(b) = f(a) + \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx$.
Going backward from a known value: $f(0) = f(2) - \int_0^2 f'(x)\,dx$.
With no elementary antiderivative, a calculator evaluates the integral; write the integral as the setup.

misconception.wrong: $f(5) = \int_2^5 f'(x)\,dx$: the integral of the derivative gives the function.
misconception.right: The integral of $f'$ gives the change in $f$. Add the known starting value: $f(5) = f(2) + \int_2^5 f'(x)\,dx$.

summary: To evaluate $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$, find an antiderivative $F$ and compute $F(b) - F(a)$. Read in context, the integral of a rate of change is the net change: $f(b) = f(a) + \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx$. Use signed areas from a graph of $f'$, an antiderivative from a formula, or a calculator when no formula exists.
